title: Nuns in the Theravada
hook: the nuns' order died out in Theravada lands; some now revive it and some do not; both views are held in good faith

segments.voice: Yesterday: pabbajja, ordaining for a while, and your line, for a while. Did you set one small thing down for a day, and notice the space it left? Day three hundred two.

A broom scrapes across a temple courtyard in Thailand, early, before the monks come back from the alms round. The woman holding it has a shaved head and wears white. She keeps eight precepts. She meditates for hours. She may have lived this way for forty years. But she isn't a nun in the full sense the old texts describe, and in Thailand the main monastic body doesn't recognize full ordination for women. Why not? Today's answer is a real disagreement, and both sides care about it deeply.
screen: `A WOMAN IN WHITE, SWEEPING AT DAWN.` → `EIGHT PRECEPTS, FORTY YEARS.` → `WHY NOT A FULL NUN?`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning. The Vinaya tells how Mahapajapati, the aunt who raised the Buddha, asked to go forth. At first he declined. Then, with Ananda speaking for her, the Buddha agreed, and the order of bhikkhunis, fully ordained nuns, began. Their voices survive in the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. For centuries the nuns' order flourished in Sri Lanka, and tradition says Sri Lankan nuns helped give ordination to women in China. Then, in a time of war, the order in Sri Lanka died out, and historians find no clear record of it continuing anywhere else in the Theravada lands. Here is the knot. The Vinaya says a woman's full ordination is given by both nuns and monks together. With no Theravada nuns left, many elders conclude it can no longer be given: the rule needs nuns, and there are none. They are guarding the code exactly as it was handed down. Others point to the nuns of East Asia, whose lineage traces back, in part, to those Sri Lankan women. In recent decades, women have been fully ordained with their help, and communities of bhikkhunis now live in Sri Lanka and in other countries. They are guarding what the Buddha himself began. In Thailand and Myanmar the main monastic bodies don't recognize these ordinations. Meanwhile, many women keep eight or ten precepts in white or pink robes, honored, practicing, teaching. Both views are held in good faith, by people who love the same teaching. The question is still open.
screen: `MAHAPAJAPATI ASKS TO GO FORTH.` · `THE ORDER FADES IN SRI LANKA.` · `THE RULE NEEDS NUNS TO ORDAIN NUNS.` · `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH IN GOOD FAITH.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION IS STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: For this sit, honor one woman who practiced. It could be Mahapajapati, who asked first. It could be Kisa Gotami, whom you met with the mustard seed. It could be a grandmother, a teacher, or the woman in white sweeping the courtyard. Hold her in mind. On each out-breath, if you like, silently wish her well: may she be at ease. Then let her go, and simply sit. The bell holds the time.
Bhikkhuni. A fully ordained nun: an order that began with the Buddha's aunt Mahapajapati, faded in Sri Lanka, and is being revived by some today.
Your line: the question is still open. Today, when you meet a disagreement, try saying both sides fairly before you say which one you lean toward. Day three hundred two.

howItsDone: In Sri Lanka some women are now fully ordained as bhikkhunis, while in Thailand, Myanmar and Sri Lanka many women live as precept-keeping renunciants (mae chi, thilashin, dasa sil mata) in white or pink robes; the main monastic bodies of Thailand and Myanmar do not recognize bhikkhuni ordination.

match.prompt: match the pieces of the story.
pairs: spoke for her to the Buddha

myth: the Buddha never allowed women to ordain
the Vinaya tells how he first declined, then agreed once Ananda spoke for Mahapajapati.
the Vinaya says nuns are ordained by nuns and monks together
that's the knot: with no Theravada nuns left, many elders say it can't be given.
every Theravada country now recognizes fully ordained nuns
some women in Sri Lanka are ordained; the main bodies in Thailand and Myanmar don't recognize it.

fork.setup: you're a Theravada elder. a sincere woman asks you for full ordination, and there are no Theravada nuns to join the ceremony. what do you do?
options: decline: the rule needs nuns, and there are none.
ordain her with the help of East Asian nuns.
either, and elders have chosen both.
fork.reveal: both answers are given today by serious, careful people. one guards the code as handed down; the other guards what the Buddha began.

original.note: Pali bhikkhunī: a fully ordained nun, the women's counterpart of bhikkhu, one who lives on alms.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism simply doesn't have nuns.
what it means: it did from the start, and whether the Theravada order can be revived is a live question.
what a scholar hears: the dispute turns on dual ordination in the Vinaya and on whether the Dharmaguptaka nuns' lineage of East Asia can stand in for a Theravada one.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): added the Buddha's initial refusal before Ananda's intervention (the Cullavagga account; the earlier text said simply 'he agreed'); hook no longer opens 'Walk into'; 'in most of the Theravada world she can't' narrowed to Thailand's main monastic body; cut the unsourced Therigatha superlative, the century dates, 'famine', 'late 1990s' and 'hundreds of bhikkhunis' from the voice and the match game.
The Cullavagga account also includes the eight 'heavy rules' (garudhamma) and a prediction about the teaching's decline; left out for length. Keeper may want them named.
Sri Lankan nuns giving ordination in China (traditionally dated to 433–434 CE): confirm framing as 'tradition says'.
Date for the end of the Sri Lankan bhikkhuni order (around the 11th century) is the usual scholarly estimate: confirm.
Revival: Sarnath 1996 and Bodh Gaya 1998 ordinations; 'hundreds of bhikkhunis in Sri Lanka' today: confirm the current figure.
Recognition status in Thailand and Myanmar: confirm it is current.
Kisa Gotami appeared earlier in the path (Camp 2); confirm the mustard-seed reference matches an earlier day.
